turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doc. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, uh, I guess the main thing, the reason I finally made the appointment—which, by the way, my wife has been on my case about for months, probably since right around Thanksgiving when we had that whole blowout about the garage, but anyway—what really brought me in is that people just keep saying I'm not listening to them. 

It's not that I don't want to listen, you know? I work at the manufacturing plant, on the production floor, and sure, it gets loud out there, but even when it's quiet, it happens. Like, my supervisor will pull me aside, look me dead in the eye, and start explaining a shift change or a new safety protocol or something. And he'll be talking straight to me, right? Just me and him. But then, maybe a minute later, I suddenly realize my brain was just... I don't even know where it went. I realize I only caught maybe half of what he said, if that. And then I have to stand there looking like an idiot and ask him to say the whole thing all over again. He gets pretty ticked off about it.

And it's not just him, it's my wife, too. She'll be sitting right across the kitchen table from me, talking about her day or telling me about the bills, and I swear I'm looking right at her, but then she stops and waits for me to answer, and I have absolutely no idea what she just said. It's causing a lot of friction, you know? Because they think I don't care or I'm ignoring them on purpose, but I'm really not, I just... I just miss half of it and I don't know why.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly describes situations where people speak directly to him (supervisor, wife) and he realizes he hasn't absorbed what they said, leading to complaints that he is not listening.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in a quiet place with no distractions—like at home in the evening—and someone is talking to you one-on-one, do you still have trouble following what they're saying, or does that mainly happen when there's background noise or other things going on around you?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, no, that's exactly it, it definitely happens when it's completely quiet, too. Like I was saying about my wife at the kitchen table. That's usually at night, right? The kids are in their rooms, the TV is off, it's just the hum of the refrigerator. It's literally as quiet as it gets in our house. And she'll be sitting right there, maybe three feet away from me. No radio, no nothing. And she'll be talking about, I don't know, her sister's upcoming visit, or maybe going over the electric bill because it was high last month, and I'm looking right at her. I'm making eye contact, nodding, doing the whole thing. 

But then... it's like a radio station losing its signal. One second I hear her saying "the due date is on the 15th," and then my brain is just... gone. I'm looking at her mouth moving, but I'm not actually hearing the words anymore. And then she stops, and I realize I've missed a solid minute of what she said. Like I mentioned, I only caught maybe half of it, if that. And I have to sit there and say, "Honey, I'm sorry, can you say that all again?" And man, she hates that. She really does. 

It's exactly the same deal with my supervisor. Even if he takes me into the little glass office on the production floor where it's soundproofed and quiet, it still happens. It's not the background noise, Doc. It's just... like I said, the whole reason I'm here is because people keep saying I'm not listening to them. They'll be talking straight to me, dead in the quiet, one-on-one, and a minute later I'm asking them to say it again because I only caught half of it. It's incredibly frustrating because I am trying, I really am, but the words just slip right past me.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly confirms that they fail to listen or process what is being said when spoken to directly, even in completely quiet, distraction-free environments.

turns.patient_response:
Yeah, no, it’s definitely not right at the very start. Like I was saying before, it’s usually after they've been going for a little bit. When my supervisor—Dave, his name is Dave, he's been there about five years longer than me—when Dave first walks up, I’m completely dialed in. Same thing with my wife. She'll sit down, she'll start talking about her sister, and I hear the beginning part. I know we're talking about her sister. But then she keeps talking, and a minute later, I'm just watching her lips move. It's like my tank only holds about sixty seconds' worth of gas for listening, and then it's empty. And then I have to do the walk of shame and ask them to say it all over again, which makes them think I wasn't paying attention from the jump, even though I was. It's just that delay, you know? I catch the start, and then a minute later I'm totally lost and asking them to repeat themselves.

I am on the floor running the stamping press, which is this massive piece of machinery, and you really have to be on your toes. You have the sheet metal coming in, you have to watch the alignment, check the pressure gauges, make sure the scrap conveyor at the back is not jamming up. And I can do that all day long. My shift is eight hours, sometimes ten if we are pulling overtime, which we have been lately because of all the supply chain stuff backing up, and I do not lose focus on that machine for a single second. If you zone out there, you could seriously get hurt, or you ruin a whole batch of expensive parts and Dave gets on your case again. So no, I am totally locked in when I am actually working on a task. 

And TV is the exact same way. I am totally fine there. Like on Sundays, they run these marathons of that show where they restore old muscle cars. I do not know if you have seen it, but they take these total rust buckets, like an old 69 Charger or something, and they completely tear them down to the bare frame, sandblast them, rebuild the carburetors, do all the custom upholstery, the whole nine yards. I can sit in my recliner and watch three or four hours of that straight, no problem at all. I do not miss a single detail of how they fix those engines. My wife actually gets mad at me for that, too, because she will say I am too focused on the TV and not paying attention to her or the stuff we need to do around the house. Which I guess brings us right back to the whole talking thing, because she will try to talk to me while the show is on and I am just glued to the screen. 

As for reading, well, I do not really read books. I have just never been a big book guy since high school, I do not have the patience to sit with a novel. But I read the sports articles on my phone, or I will go down a huge rabbit hole reading about fishing gear or looking up specs for truck parts for an hour, and I do not lose my place or forget what I am reading at all. 

It really is just when people are actually standing there talking to me. I do not know why it is different, but if my hands are busy or I am watching a process happen, my brain stays right exactly where it is supposed to be. It is just the conversations that just slip right out of my head.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies having trouble sustaining attention on tasks like working, watching TV, or reading articles, stating he is 'completely fine' and 'totally locked in'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear ringing, buzzing, whistling, or any other sounds in your ears when nobody is talking to you—like when you're just sitting quietly by yourself?

No, no, nothing like that. Which, honestly, you'd probably expect I would, right? Given where I work and all. I mean, the stamping plant is incredibly loud. You've got these massive presses coming down with tons of force, metal clanging on metal, the scrap bins getting dumped, the air compressors hissing all day long. It is an absolute racket in there. 

But the company is super strict about safety gear—you know, OSHA regulations and all that—so management makes sure we always have to wear these little orange foam earplugs. You have to roll them up real tight between your fingers and stick them deep in there, and then they expand. But I guess I got lucky there. 

When I'm just sitting out in the garage by myself, maybe having a cold beer after a long ten-hour shift, it's completely silent. Well, I mean, obviously I can hear the neighbor's dog barking two houses down, or the chest freezer humming in the corner, but inside my own head? In my actual ears? No, no extra noises at all. Just regular old quiet. Which is a relief, honestly, because my brain is always going a mile a minute anyway with a hundred different thoughts, so if I had some kind of constant buzzing in my ears on top of all that, I think I'd go absolutely crazy. But no, to answer your question, no ringing at all.
